title: Psalm 73: Envying the Wicked, Finding God
summary: Asaph confesses that he nearly lost his footing when he envied the prosperity of the wicked, who seemed healthy, carefree, and arrogant while he suffered for keeping his heart pure. The problem troubled him until he entered God's sanctuary and saw their end. He ends by confessing that God holds his hand, guides him, and is his portion forever, and that nearness to God is his good.
story: Psalm 73 opens Book III of the Psalter (Psalms 73 to 89) and begins a collection of eleven psalms attributed to Asaph (73 to 83; Psalm 50 is the only other). Book II ended with the soaring royal hopes of Psalm 72. Book III opens by facing the gap between promise and experience: God is said to be good to Israel, but the wicked flourish and the faithful suffer. That question hangs over the whole of Book III, which moves through the ruins of the temple (Psalms 74 and 79) and ends with the lament over the failed Davidic covenant (Psalm 89). Psalm 73 wrestles with the problem on a personal scale before the book takes it up on a national one. Its question, why the wicked prosper, is the same one that drives Psalm 37, Job, and Habakkuk.
historical: The heading reads “A Psalm of Asaph.” Asaph was a Levite whom David appointed as a leader of temple music (1 Chronicles 15:17; 16:4-5), and his descendants continued as a guild of singers for centuries, still appearing after the exile (Ezra 2:41; Nehemiah 7:44). A psalm of Asaph may therefore be by Asaph himself or, more likely for many of these psalms, by a member of the guild that bore his name. Psalm 73 contains no clear historical reference, and scholars date it anywhere from the monarchy to after the exile. Its concern with the prosperity of the wicked and its wisdom vocabulary have led many to classify it as a wisdom psalm, and its setting in the sanctuary (verse 17) suggests the speaker was someone who had access to the temple, fitting a Levitical singer.
cultural:
Much of Israel's wisdom teaching held that the righteous prosper and the wicked come to ruin (Psalm 1; Proverbs 10). The speaker's crisis arises because life seemed to contradict that teaching. The wicked he describes wear pride like a necklace and violence like a garment (verse 6), images drawn from clothing and jewelry that displayed status. Their well-fed bodies (verse 4) were, in a world of frequent hunger, a mark of wealth. Washing one's hands in innocence (verse 13) recalls rituals of purity and declarations of innocence (Deuteronomy 21:6-7; Psalm 26:6).

The sanctuary in verse 17 was the temple in Jerusalem, the place of sacrifice, prayer, and the reading of Israel's story. What the speaker saw there is not described, whether a vision, the hearing of Scripture, worship with God's people, or simply time in God's presence. Verse 26 calls God the speaker's portion, echoing the Levites, who received no share of the land because the LORD himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20; Deuteronomy 10:9).
literary: The psalm is framed by two statements about what is good. It begins with “Surely God is good to Israel” (verse 1) and ends with “it is good to draw near to God” (verse 28), a movement from a creed held at a distance to a truth known personally. The word surely (Hebrew akh) marks three turning points: the opening confession (verse 1), the moment of despair, “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure” (verse 13), and the reversal, “Surely You set them on slick ground” (verse 18). The psalm divides at verse 17, the visit to the sanctuary. Before it the speaker looks at the wicked; after it he looks at God. Verses 2 and 18 match: the speaker's feet nearly slipped, but it is the wicked who stand on slick ground. The wicked are described at length, and the confession of verses 23 to 26, with its I am always with You, answers the whole problem by relocating the speaker's good.

outline.t: The confession: God is good to Israel
In the sanctuary: their end discerned
It is good to draw near to God

doctrines.note: The psalm faces the apparent injustice of the world squarely. Its answer isn't that the wicked never prosper but that their prosperity is short and their end is ruin, while God's care for his people is lasting.

The turning point comes in the sanctuary, the place of prayer and worship. Coming before God doesn't erase the problem, but it changes the angle of vision, setting present experience in the light of God's presence and his final judgment.
Verses 24 and 26 speak of God receiving the speaker in glory and being his portion forever. Whatever their exact scope, they ground hope beyond present circumstances, in God himself.

words.note: Akh, surely, truly, or only. A small particle that structures the psalm, it opens verses 1, 13, and 18, marking a confession of faith, a moment of despair, and the discovery of the wicked's end.

Qana, to be jealous or envious. The same root can describe God's zeal for his people, but here it is the corrosive envy that nearly causes the speaker to fall. The psalm names envy as a spiritual danger, not just an emotion.
Acharit, end, outcome, or latter part. In verse 17 the speaker discerns the end of the wicked. Wisdom literature often insists that a life must be judged by its end, not by its middle.

Cheleq, portion or share. It is used of an allotment of land or plunder. In verse 26 God himself is the speaker's portion forever, echoing the Levites, whose inheritance was the LORD rather than a tract of land.

christ: The New Testament doesn't quote Psalm 73 directly, and its connection to Jesus is thematic. Jesus warned that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions (Luke 12:15), and his story of the rich man and Lazarus turns on the same reversal of fortunes the psalm describes (Luke 16:19-31). The confession that God holds the believer's hand and will afterward receive him in glory takes on its fullest meaning in Christ, who promised that no one can snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28) and who went ahead to prepare a place for his people (John 14:2-3). Christians read the psalm's hope of being always with God in light of the resurrection, where that nearness becomes permanent.

hard.q: Does verse 24 teach life after death, which the Old Testament often seems to leave unclear?
hard.a: Scholars disagree. Many read “later receive me in glory” as a hope of being taken to God after death, noting that the Hebrew verb for receive or take (laqach) is used when God took Enoch (Genesis 5:24) and Elijah (2 Kings 2:3), and that verse 26 speaks of God as the speaker's portion forever even when flesh and heart fail. Others think the verse means that God will restore the speaker to honor in this life after his present humiliation, since much of the Old Testament speaks of the dead as going to Sheol without clear hope of glory. A middle view holds that the psalm reaches toward a hope it does not fully define: communion with God is so real that death cannot be its end. Christians read the verse in light of the New Testament's clearer teaching on resurrection, while acknowledging that the Old Testament's hope develops over time.

questions: Where are you tempted to envy people who seem to prosper without God? What does that envy do to your faith?
The speaker's perspective changed when he entered the sanctuary. What practices help you see your circumstances in God's light?
Verse 25 asks, “Whom have I in heaven but You?” What would change in your life if God were truly your portion?
